Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

vignette:
Amara Osei-Bonsu is a fifty-four-year-old Ghanaian-American federal judge, married for twenty-six years, who presented for psychological assessment following a referral from her primary care physician. She is precise in her speech and composed in her bearing, though there are moments during the intake when her composure falters in ways that seem to surprise even her - a sudden stillness, a brief disconnection in her eyes, as though she has stepped briefly behind glass.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Amara was taken from the parking structure beneath her courthouse by two men. What followed, over the course of several hours in an undisclosed location, constituted systematic physical torture. The men restrained her - wrists bound, body pinned - and subjected her to prolonged physical assault. One of them wore a heavy, sweet-musky cologne that saturated the air of the confined space. Throughout, she was aware of his breathing close to her face: labored, rhythmic, intimate in the worst possible way. She survived. The perpetrators were eventually identified and are awaiting trial in a jurisdiction that requires her recusal, a fact she finds both a relief and a source of private anguish.

In the weeks after the event, Amara noticed that her memory of what happened was strange in a way she struggled to articulate. When she tried to sit down and deliberately reconstruct the sequence - as she might reconstruct the facts of a case - she found the memory oddly inaccessible, as though it had been filed somewhere she could not locate. There were portions she simply could not retrieve at all, no matter how methodically she approached them, and this frightened her in a way she had not anticipated. More unsettling still was the quality of what she could access: she had come to describe the memory, haltingly, as feeling like something that happened to a woman she had read about rather than to herself. It was not that she doubted it occurred. It was that the experience felt authored by a stranger. She found this dissociation deeply disorienting and had told no one about it, not even her husband Kofi, because she was certain that articulating it would make her sound as though she had lost her capacity for rational thought - a capacity that was, in her mind, inseparable from who she was.

Amara returned to the bench within six weeks, which her colleagues interpreted as remarkable resilience. What they did not see was what happened in the courtroom itself. On two occasions, a male attorney appeared wearing a cologne - dense, sweet, slightly animalic - that bore a resemblance to what she had smelled that day. Both times, Amara felt something seize in her chest. She continued to conduct the proceedings, but she described those hours afterward as feeling scraped hollow. She began arriving earlier than necessary to air out the courtroom and had quietly asked her clerk to seat cologne-wearing parties at greater distance from the bench, framing it as a sensitivity. The explanation was not entirely false, but it was not the truth either.

Outside the courthouse, certain moments had become unbearable in ways she could not always predict. Her husband, a warm and physically affectionate man, had taken to reaching for her hand or placing an arm around her shoulders, and on several occasions when he did so unexpectedly - when she felt the weight of his arm pinning hers against her side - she had pulled away sharply. She had not explained why. The distance between them had grown in the way that distances do when neither person names what is happening, and Kofi had begun to ask, quietly and with evident pain, whether she still wanted him near. She did. She was certain of that. But the feeling of being held down, even gently, even lovingly, had become something her body treated as a signal she could not override.

What finally brought Amara to seek help was a moment in her own courtroom three weeks ago. A bailiff placed a steadying hand on a defendant's shoulder, and the sound of the man's audible, effortful breathing filled the brief silence of the room. Amara gripped the edge of the bench and did not move for several seconds. She was afraid someone had noticed. She came to her first appointment hoping, above everything else, that she had not permanently lost access to herself - and terrified that she had.
